newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia marks Christmas as Orthodox faith revives.
newsitem.headline: Russia marks Christmas as Orthodox faith revives.

text.p: Millions of Russians attended Christmas mass on Tuesday, celebrating Orthodox rites that are flourishing, amid poverty and social chaos, after seven decades of Soviet religious repression.

Patriarch Alexiy II, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, chided the government for its failure to meet promises to pay unpaid wages and pensions before officiating at a packed midnight service in Moscow's ornate Epiphany church.

He will conduct afternoon mass at the newly rebuilt Christ the Saviour cathedral, near the Kremlin, which has risen dramatically in just two years on the site of an identical 19th century predecessor blown up on Stalin's orders in 1931.

The massive church, which should be completed this year, is a concrete testament to the resurrection of the faith across the nation. Some data suggest up to half Russia's 150 million people are active Orthodox believers despite years of official atheism.
President Boris Yeltsin, an ex-communist who has encouraged the revival of the thousand year-old state church, is not due to attend public services after catching a "heavy cold" on Monday.
A Kremlin spokesman told Reuters on Tuesday he would spend part of the day in bed at his Gorky-9 residence near Moscow.
His office said on Monday the illness had nothing to do with the 65-year-old leader's heart bypass operation last November.
Michael DeBakey, the Texan surgeon who advised on Yeltsin's doctors, told Reuters he was recovering "right on schedule".
In a statement on Monday, Yeltsin praised the church for affirming the "high ideals of spirituality and the achievement of unity and concord among the peoples of the Russian state."
In 1992, he decreed Orthodox Christmas a public holiday. But New Year, celebrated last week, remains, as engineered by Soviet leaders, the main winter festival of feasting and gift-giving.
The communists brought the secular calendar in line with the West but the Orthodox Church continues to use the old calendar, on which Christmas falls 13 days later than for western creeds.
In a Christmas Eve address, Patriarch Alexiy appealed to the Kremlin to remember the tens of millions of Russia's poor and to tackle the problem of unpaid wages and pensions.
"We urge the leadership of the country...to recognise the urgent need for resolution of this problem," he said.
Neglected churches across the country have benefited from the donations of some of Russia's new rich minority.

But there has been criticism of the millions of dollars spent on rebuilding Christ the Saviour, albeit private money, when much of the nation is on the breadline. The white-bearded patriarch decried the growing gap between rich and poor.
"At all times the Church has been and remains on the side of the weak and the unfortunate," he said.

As in tsarist and Soviet times, however, the church is closely tied to the state. Secular leaders, including the now fiercely nationalistic Communist party, have sought to exploit the church's authority to bolster their own legitimacy.

This new state Orthodoxy has worried some of the substantial Moslem minority and heightened calls for autonomy in predominantly Moslem provinces. Demands for an Islamic republic were one factor in the recently ended war in Chechnya.
Buddhism is also an officially recognised religion in parts of Siberia and the Far East. Many Jews, oppressed for centuries by tsars and communists alike, continue to emigrate to Israel.
